item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers won 100 games this season. They claimed the National League West division yet again. But, after reaching the National League Championship Series, their World Series three-peat bid flamed out in a sweep to the Brewers.
In the wake of their elimination, The California Post graded the season of every player on the Dodgers’ roster.
First up, the offense, which ranked top-five in the regular season in scoring, batting average and OPS –– but faltered in the playoffs and was shut down in the NLCS.
Shohei Ohtani: F
To be clear: The two-way star was the second-best player in the National League this year, hitting 30 home runs and posting a sub-2.00 ERA in 14 starts on the mound. Even in a relatively down year for him, he finished fifth in the majors in Fangraphs’ version of wins above replacement. He remains, undoubtedly, MLB’s foremost star player and the Dodgers’ most potent weapon.
But that is why the way his season finished was such a failure.
What mattered most for the Dodgers this year was having Ohtani –– especially as a hitter –– at full strength come the postseason. By trying to play through right arm and left knee injuries, he wasn’t.
And while there is blame to be shared for the way his health was managed, from team decision-makers to Ohtani himself, it is impossible not to second-guess what this October might have looked like if the slugger was in a better place physically.
Instead, his .192 playoff batting average was not nearly enough to save the Dodgers’ offense. In the end, his one big swing in Game 4 of the NLCS was too little, too late. Moving forward, he and the team might have to reimagine his usage to avoid a repeat of this year. Because, especially as the rest of the roster gets older, they can’t afford another late-season injury crisis like this with Ohtani again.
Freddie Freeman: B-
In his 17th MLB season, Freeman earned his 10th career All-Star selection, finished 13th in the majors in total hits, and continued his march towards Cooperstown. But, the 37-year-old also saw his total production (measured by WAR) decline for a fourth-straight year.
He hit just one regular-season home run after July 4. His batting average dropped from .306 to .288 amid a knee issue in September. And despite a couple big swings in the playoffs, he finished October just 5-for-29. Now, entering the final season of his contract but intending to play at least a couple more beyond that, the Dodgers will have to start deciding if he will remain in their longer-term plans.
Mookie Betts: B
What was shaping up to be a lost year for Betts instead finished with signs of renewed life. On Aug. 4, he was hitting .223 with a .670 OPS. In 46 games after that, he posted a .315/.399/.562 slash line while nearly doubling his home run total from 13 to 23.
It was the best he had looked since the first half of 2024 and a reminder that, even at 34 years old now, there is a superstar level he is still capable of reaching. The Dodgers will be hoping that’s what they get from him in 2027.
Max Muncy: B+
This was a resurgent season for Muncy, who returned to the All-Star Game for the first time since 2021 while hitting for his highest average (.252) since 2018. He stayed healthy, playing 149 games and hitting 29 home runs.
He also improved his defense, earning a nod as a Gold Glove finalist at third base. He’ll be back at third next season, in the final guaranteed year of his contract.
Andy Pages: A-
Pages didn’t sustain his torrid pace from early in the year (he had a .303 average and .899 OPS on May 27, then a .254 average and .751 OPS thereafter) but still cemented himself as the youngest core piece of the roster, earning an All-Star nod with his improved approach and stellar center-field defense. His postseason was an improvement from 2025 too.
Teoscar Hernández: C
A late surge at the plate helped save some of Hernández’s season-long numbers (.267 average, .759 OPS) following a prolonged slump upon his return from a hamstring strain.
But after being bandied around in potential trade discussions last offseason, it’s possible his future with the club could be in question again this winter.
Kyle Tucker: D
The only thing saving this from being an F is the way Tucker finished his otherwise dismal debut season, highlighted by a team-best .333 batting average in the playoffs. Still, the 29-year-old played nowhere near expectations after his $240 offseason signing, setting career-lows in average (.233), OPS (.715) and home runs (17).
The Dodgers will be desperate for him to return to form next year, when he will play an even more vital role in their still-aging lineup. If not, those $60 million player options in 2028 and 2029 will start to feel like poison pills.
Will Smith: C
This is a relatively incomplete grade, given Smith was limited to just 73 games by a three-month neck injury. But even when he did play, the veteran backstop took a step back. His .260 average and .781 OPS were the second-lowest marks of his career (ahead of only 2024). He went just 3-for-31 in the playoffs, salvaging only so much with his Game 3 double in the NLCS.
Tommy Edman: C
After missing the start of the year recovering from ankle surgery, Edman did little more than meet expectations in his utility role with the Dodgers. He was a streaky .247 hitter, finishing with a just-about-league-average .714 OPS. He played good defense and shifted around the diamond. But any more profound impact was limited.
Kiké Hernández: C
Injuries derailed Hernández’s year. And though he had another big October moment –– hitting a home run off Chris Sale in the NLDS –– there was little else to take from his 13th big-league campaign. Once again a free agent, he will represent one of the more intriguing questions of the Dodgers’ winter.
Each of the last three offseasons, they have re-signed him to a one-year deal. Whether they do so again could be a signal for how much, or little, of a shake-up they’re planning for next year.
Dalton Rushing: B
For Rushing, it was a year of promising highs (seven home runs in March/April, .288 batting average in July) and frustrating lows (emotional outbursts early in the year, his spat with Ohtani on the mound in June, and a late-season elbow injury that sidelined him for the playoffs) for the former top prospect. He has more to prove entering Year 3 in 2027.
Alex Freeland: C
Another ex-prospect, Freeland didn’t capitalize on increased opportunity this year, hitting just .234 with only 13 extra-base hits in 89 games. Though still only 25, he remains on the fringes of the team’s long-term plans.
Alex Call: C
The backup outfielder survived the trade deadline. But after hitting just .233 in his reserve role, he might not be a lock to return in his reserve role next year.
Josue De Paula: B+
In his brief MLB debut, De Paula did everything right as a hitter, reaching base at a .500 clip in 11 regular-season games before drawing two key walks as a pinch-hitter in October. Offensively, he seems ready for everyday big-league duties. But the gigantic question mark about his outfield defense leaves his 2027 role unclear entering the winter.
Hyeseong Kim: D
Time will tell if the Dodgers still see something in Kim. But the way he was buried in triple-A this year, after playing just 43 games in the majors in April and May, was not a good sign as he enters the final guaranteed year of his contract.
Hunter Feduccia: B
The former Dodgers farmhand returned to the club in a deadline day trade and was perfectly adequate as the backup catcher over the final couple months of the season. Whether there’s a role for him in the organization again next year remains to be seen.
Miguel Rojas: A
We’re grading on a curve here, in what was a fittingly effective send-off season for the now-retired veteran infielder. Rojas did his job by menacing left-handed pitching (.293 average against them), playing stout defense and serving as a vocal leader in the Dodgers’ star-studded clubhouse. After an accomplished 13-year MLB career –– highlighted by his season-saving home run in Game 7 of last year’s World Series –– his presence will be missed in the clubhouse.

Los Angeles Dodgers outfielder Alex Call argued that scandalous commercials are getting in the way of passing down his love of baseball to his son.
“Can we please get the soft porn ads off playoff broadcasts, TBS, Fox, NBC, @MLB?” Call, 32, posted via X on Wednesday, October 14. “My son wants to watch baseball with Dada, but how do I justify that when a half-naked women could come on screen anytime?? This is America’s Pastime. Parents shouldn’t have to worry about this.”
Alex and his wife, Samantha, share a son born in 2023 whose name has been kept private and daughter Reverie, 9 months.
The Dodgers player was responding to a social media post that wondered if Major League Baseball is interested in getting “more kids” watching the sport.
“Maybe start with the commercials,” Utah-based entrepreneur Taylor Murphy wrote. “Watching the playoffs tonight with my kids and here’s the rundown: Megan Fox selling ED pills in a red bodysuit. The scariest movie trailer you’ve ever seen. Sydney Sweeney in zero clothes promoting betting on sports.”
He continued, “Leagues can’t figure out why kids don’t watch. You don’t need a Nickelodeon game. You’re not the Savannah Bananas. Just show baseball in a way I can leave on in my house.”
Murphy’s post has gone viral since being posted Monday, October 12, earning over 31,000 likes.
Sweeney’s ad campaign for sports trading app NOVIG has been particularly controversial. The commercials, which have aired throughout the 2026 MLB Playoffs, feature the actress, 29, in various states of undress with sports equipment covering her naked body.
Sharon Stone, who costarred with Sweeney on HBO’s Euphoria, urged the young star to “take responsibility for her actions.”
“It is up to me to be a cheerleader for the women who have made it through and become champions in women’s sports,” Stone, 68, told People last month.
Call played in 88 games as a reserve outfielder for the Dodgers during the 2026 season. He has yet to see any postseason action.
The athlete shared photos of his family of four to celebrate Mother’s Day in May.
“You are the heart of our family,” Call wrote via Instagram. “When I’m gone for a week at a time, you’re home grinding it out, taking care of our kids with a kind of love and sweetness that bring me joy every time I think about it. Our family doesn’t work without you, and I don’t know what I would do without you. You’re my best friend. You make me happier than I ever knew was possible. There’s no one I’d rather do life with, raise these kids with, or come home to.”
The Dodgers will attempt to avoid being swept by the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series in Los Angeles on Thursday, October 15.

item.content:encoded:
Los fanáticos de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles no permitieron que los recientes comentarios de Alex Call sobre los comerciales de "pornografía suave" afectaran su apoyo hacia él antes del Juego 3 de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional el miércoles, ya que lo vitorearon como de costumbre durante la presentación de los jugadores.
Call, de 32 años, causó revuelo esta semana cuando comentó una publicación viral de X que criticaba los anuncios que se emiten durante los partidos de los playoffs de la MLB, afirmando que los padres no deberían tener que preocuparse de que "una mujer semidesnuda" aparezca en la pantalla en cualquier momento.
Las declaraciones del jardinero derecho de los Dodgers se producen tras semanas de controversia en torno a las atrevidas campañas publicitarias de la actriz de primera línea Sydney Sweeney con la empresa de pronósticos Novig, en las que aparece con poca ropa, y en algunos casos completamente desnuda, mientras se cubre estratégicamente con equipamiento deportivo.
Esta semana, los aficionados que sintonizaban los playoffs de la MLB se vieron expuestos a un anuncio sobre disfunción eréctil protagonizado por Megan Fox y el spot de Novig de Sweeney, respaldado por los dueños de la compañía, lo que provocó varias quejas de padres en internet.
Una de esas quejas llamó la atención de Call, quien respondió con su propia publicación argumentando que la MLB no necesitaba trucos para atraer a los espectadores más jóvenes, sino simplemente una transmisión que las familias pudieran seguir viendo cómodamente.
Dodgers outfielder Alex Call was cheered during the player introductions of Game 3 of the NLCS in the wake of his recent comments about MLB ads. https://t.co/9pePuNriDK pic.twitter.com/lXB5pT8hAZ
— California Post Sports (@capostsports) October 15, 2026
"¿Podemos, por favor, quitar los anuncios sugerentes de las transmisiones de los playoffs en TBS, Fox, NBC y la MLB?", escribió Call. "Mi hijo quiere ver béisbol con papá, pero ¿cómo lo justifico cuando una mujer semidesnuda podría aparecer en pantalla en cualquier momento? Este es el pasatiempo nacional de Estados Unidos. Los padres no deberían tener que preocuparse por esto".
Call recibió mucho apoyo por su mensaje, con muchos fanáticos de acuerdo con su postura y exigiendo que algo cambiara, y esos sentimientos hacia la estrella de los Dodgers ciertamente se transmitieron a las gradas el miércoles antes del choque del Juego 3 de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional de su equipo contra los Milwaukee Brewers.
En un video grabado desde las gradas y publicado en X, se podía ver a Call, quien no había aparecido en un partido de postemporada hasta el momento, a pesar de estar en la plantilla activa de los Dodgers, alineándose junto a sus compañeros en el campo del Dodger Stadium mientras se leían los nombres de los jugadores.
Tras una gran ovación para el tercera base de los Dodgers, Max Clusty, el nombre de Call fue el siguiente en la lista a ser anunciado, y se podía oír claramente a los aficionados dándole una cálida bienvenida mientras él saludaba cortésmente a la multitud.
Poco después, algunos aficionados acusaron a Joe Davis, de FOX Sports, de haber hecho la "peor narración de la historia" tras ser sorprendido en plena presentación cuando Jackson Chourio conectó un jonrón en el primer lanzamiento del tercer partido de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional.
El comentarista de FOX estaba dando sus palabras de apertura antes del partido cuando Chourio sorprendió al primer lanzamiento del juego, enviando una bola rápida de 98 mph de Blake Snell a las gradas del jardín derecho para darle a los Brewers una ventaja de 1-0.
Desafortunadamente para todos los seguidores de Los Ángeles, el equipo no pudo lograr la victoria contra los Brewers, cayendo 6-2 y quedando abajo 3-0 en la serie al mejor de siete, al borde de la eliminación.
Eso convierte el cuarto partido de esta noche (jueves 15 de octubre), programado en el Dodger Stadium, en una victoria imprescindible para los Dodgers si quieren tener alguna posibilidad de lograr una remontada memorable, ya que otra derrota confirmaría el final de su temporada.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers outfielder Alex Call called on Major League Baseball and its broadcast partners to remove what he called “soft porn” ads from 2026 playoff telecasts.
The callout was in response to an MLB fan on X, Taylor Murphy, who went viral after posting that the MLB could get younger kids watching if it aired ads that made parents comfortable leaving the TV on unattended.
“Wanna get more kids watching baseball? Maybe start with the commercials,” Murphy said.
When trying to watch the program with his kids, ads of Megan Fox selling erectile dysfunction pills in a red bodysuit, “the scariest movie trailer you’ve ever seen,” and Sydney Sweeney in “zero clothes” promoting sports betting aired between plays.
He continued, saying the MLB doesn’t need a Savannah Bananas gimmick or a Nickelodeon-style game. The league can simply “show baseball in a way I can leave on in my house.”
Call, a father of two, agreed with Murphy on X.
“Can we please get the soft porn ads off playoff broadcasts—TBS, Fox, NBC—@MLB?” Call wrote. “My son wants to watch baseball with Dada, but how do I justify that when a half-naked woman could come on screen anytime?”
This is the sports world’s latest snub of Sweeney over her ad for the sports-prediction market Novig. She’s filmed talking about the “just sports” betting platform and covering her naked body with various sports equipment.
Female athletes and celebrities have responded, calling the ad “damaging” to women’s sports.
Four-time Olympic swimming champion Ariarne Titmus said it “monetizes” women’s bodies, while former UCLA gymnast Gracie Kramer said female athletes have long fought to be seen for their performance rather than their bodies.
Sprinter Amy Hunt, water-polo player Tilly Kearns, and rugby player Sofie Fella also all pushed back on the ad.
Novig CEO Jack Fortinsky defended the campaign, saying the company is “hugely supportive of women’s sports,” never intended to portray female athletes, and viewed Sweeney simply as an actress delivering a sports-focused message.
Though she hasn’t responded to Call directly, Sweeney publicly said she filmed the ad because she believes in the company’s leadership and message.
Murphy and Call received mixed responses, with parents supporting the take and others saying kids “aren’t the target audience” and the MLB doesn’t control the ads that play between programming. To which Murphy replied with a highlighted screenshot from a 2024 MLB advertising standards document.
The MLB reserves the right to “reject or instruct” any partner to cease the use of any ad “during, or in connection with, any Baseball Programming Transmission,” according to the document.
Call concluded his X rant with, “This is America’s Pastime. Parents shouldn’t have to worry about this.”

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers, who are currently trailing the Milwaukee Brewers two games to none in the National League Championship Series, decided not to include outfielder Alex Call on their postseason roster after he hit .233 over 88 regular-season appearances in 2026.
However, he continues to watch games – but has a particular problem with some of the advertisements being shown.
In a comment on social media that’s since gone viral, Call has expressed his disdain for the ongoing Novig advertising campaign, which features a scantily clad Sydney Sweeney.
Los Angeles Dodgers Outfielder Alex Call Blasts MLB Broadcasts Over Advertising
In a comment on social media that has since gone viral, Call made it clear that he believes the advertising campaign isn’t appropriate for audiences that include kids.
“Can we please get the soft p*** ads off playoff broadcasts, TBS, Fox, NBC, @MLB? My son wants to watch baseball with Dada, but how do I justify that when a half-naked women could come on screen anytime?? This is America’s Pastime. Parents shouldn’t have to worry about this,” Call wrote on X, formerly known as Twitter.
Immediately, the responses started coming through from fans, many of which voiced agreement with what he had to say.
One fan said, “Not to mention being 31 watching the game with your dad and those ads come on. Just awkward.”
Another fan said, “You are 💯% right. These p********** ads has no business playing on our television screens in front of our children.”
“Thanks Alex. I’m no saint, but my kids are. And it pisses me off when those commercials come on. My son loves the dodgers, watches more than I do, but now I have to be cautious during commercial breaks. It’s BS,” said another fan.
This fan said, “Amen. Those ads have no place on TV especially with young children watching.”
“You have a high enough profile, along with that viral post. If you call for a 1-inning parent boycott to make a point maybe they will listen,” said another fan in response.
Finally, this fan said, “Yes! I have 3 teen/young adult boys and a pre-teen at home who watch baseball. Keep it family friendly! Even if they weren’t watching, I don’t want to see that!”
Alex Call Is Coming Off His First Full Year In Los Angeles
Call was drafted by the Chicago White Sox in the third round in 2016 and reached the majors with Cleveland in 2022, appearing in 12 games before being designated for assignment.
The Washington Nationals claimed Call off waivers that August, and he spent parts of the next three seasons with the club. He was traded to the Dodgers at the 2025 deadline after a strong 2024 stretch in which he hit .343 over 30 games.
Call appeared in 38 regular-season games for Los Angeles in 2025 and played throughout the postseason, including the World Series. In the 88 games he played in 2026, he hit one home run with 26 RBI.

My son wants to watch baseball with Dada, but how do I justify that when a half-naked women could come on screen anytime?? This is America's Pastime. Parents shouldn't have to worry about this," Call wrote on social media.

"Thanks Alex. I'm no saint, but my kids are. And it annoys me when those commercials come on. My son loves the dodgers, watches more than I do, but now I have to be cautious during commercial breaks," one fan wrote on X.

MINNEAPOLIS -- Los Angeles Dodgers outfielder Kyle Tucker was removed from Monday's game against the Minnesota Twins in the second inning because of low back spasms.
Tucker walked with one out in the second and ran lightly to second base on Tommy Edman's single to right field. Then, Tucker was replaced by pinch runner Alex Call. Tucker stayed in the dugout, standing up next to dugout fence before heading into the clubhouse after the inning was over.
"I really felt it when I went out for defense in between innings in the first," Tucker said. "Went out there and just tried to hope that it could kind of calm down, or go away or something and I could just keep playing through it. ... On the bases and stuff, it was kind of still sticking around, still kind of there."
Manager Dave Roberts said he considered Tucker day-to-day. The outfielder said, "just got to kind of see how it goes tomorrow," regarding his status.
After signing a four-year, $240 million contract with Los Angeles in January, Tucker has played in 75 of the Dodgers' 79 games this season. But he has hit just .234 with six home runs and 40 RBIs. The .234 average is his lowest since hitting .141 in 28 games as a rookie in Houston in 2018. He has hit at least 22 homers in each of the past five seasons.
The Dodgers also pulled catcher Dalton Rushing in the bottom of the third to rule out a concussion. Roberts said Rushing passed concussion testing, but the catcher has to retake the test 24 hours later and probably will be out of Tuesday's lineup. He was replaced by Chuckie Robinson and Roberts said the team probably would add another player in case Rushing is unavailable.
Los Angeles was already without No. 1 catcher Will Smith, who is on the 10-day IL because of neck inflammation.

Now that the 2026 MLB regular season is done, Sony made one last ratings tweak for many of the players across the league on October 2. The October MLB The Show 26 ratings update saw Mookie Betts & Cade Smith rise to join the other Diamonds in the game.

Smith, meanwhile, notched 41 saves and struck out 107 batters over 74 innings this season for the Guardians.
Fernando Tatis Jr. moved up three points between the last update and now. Tatis Jr., before the start of the playoffs, hit five home runs and nine extra-base hits in the last 15 games of the regular season for San Diego.
Elly De La Cruz, who had eight extra-base hits in the final two weeks, moved to 87 OVR, a +2 OVR increase. He moved there, along with NL Wild Card hero Michael Harris II.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA.
One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered.
Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula called upon
Catchers (2): Will Smith, Hunter Feduccia
For some reason, the Dodgers decided to carry three catchers on their Wild Card and NLDS rosters last year — Smith, Dalton Rushing, and Ben Rortvedt — but adjusted ahead of the NLCS by shedding Rushing, who received just one at-bat in the NLDS but otherwise rode the bench.
Rortvedt didn't get a start or even substitution after Game 2 of the NLDS with Smith slowly coming back from injury at the beginning of the postseason. Feduccia figures to play a similar break-glass-in-case-of-emergency role. As a lefty, he could get a start and then an early pull depending on matchups but, barring disaster, it's mostly going to be Smith's show.
Designated hitters (2): Shohei Ohtani, Josue De Paula
The Dodgers clearly want to find a way to bring De Paula with them in October, even if only as a lingering threat on their bench. They're reportedly not entertaining putting him in the outfield at all, and it's not hard to see why. Even if they're confident they'll be able to fix his defense in time, they can't afford any leakage in the postseason.
Ohtani is still shaking off the cobwebs from his 15-day IL stint. He picked up a few hits with promising exit velocity in his return against the San Diego Padres and later against the San Francisco Giants, but there are still question marks around what version of him we might see this postseason.
Infielders (6): Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Tommy Edman, Max Muncy, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández
A notable exclusion here is Hyeseong Kim. Although he's in the running to get a spot on the bench and exclusively come into games to pinch-run or for reassurances on defense, there's still a chance he doesn't make the roster if the Dodgers are set on carrying 13 pitchers. Edman and Hernández, though lacking the same speed as Kim, can still offer the same defensive versatility.
Outfielders (3): Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández
Pages might've found himself in the same boat as Ohtani, but he announced his return to the Dodgers after a month-long IL stint in a big way, hitting .333 with a 1.180 OPS, two homers, and five RBI against the Padres and Giants. No doubt Dave Roberts and Andrew Friedman breathed a massive sigh of relief.
Alex Call will be the odd man out. He was on all four of LA's playoff rosters last year and received sporadic appearances throughout the month, but that was when Michael Conforto was still on the payroll. Tucker and Hernández have certainly had their ups-and-downs this season, but the Dodgers would never seriously consider leaving them out.
Starters (4): Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal, Tyler Glasnow
There's not much to say about what's probably the best rotation going into the postseason. Snell and Glasnow have both battled injury this season but came back when the Dodgers needed them most. It might be too much to ask that any of Yamamoto, Snell, or Glasnow replicate their dominance from last year, but they'll certainly try.
Relievers: (9): Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Justin Wrobleski, Edwin Díaz, Kris Bubic, Edgardo Henriquez
Just like 2025, this is where things get dicey. The Dodgers' bullpen isn't quite as banged up or as unreliable as they were last year, but they're not the air-tight, bulletproof coterie that their combined salaries suggest they should be. Henriquez will be coming straight off of the IL to rejoin the team in the NLDS, and Díaz, Sasaki, and Scott are all woefully unpredictable.
There is some thought that the Dodgers might carry eight relievers instead of nine, to free up a spot on the position player side for a guy like Kim. In this scenario, we'll stick with them taking nine. If not, Bubic is the most obvious cut. Last one in, first one out.

SAN FRANCISCO -- With another 162 regular-season games in the books, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts has again found himself in rarefied air.
The Dodgers' 5-1 victory over the Giants in 10 innings on Sunday afternoon at Oracle Park -- keyed by Alex Call's go-ahead double and a three-run blast from Andy Pages -- secured a 100-win campaign, their fifth in the past seven full-length seasons and their sixth with Roberts at the helm.
Roberts joins Hall of Famers Bobby Cox and Joe McCarthy as the only managers with six 100-win seasons.
"I guess I'm in some rare air, some good company," said Roberts, who in June reached 1,000 career managerial wins faster than any other manager. "A lot of good players, a great organization, and it's not easy to win 100 games. And so there's a lot of things that we had to go through this year, and we just continue to remain steadfast and play on. And so, yeah, that's something to be proud of."
The last three seasons in which the Dodgers did not win 100 games -- 2025, '24 and the pandemic-shortened '20 campaign -- they won the World Series. In their 11 previous 100-win seasons, they failed to win a championship.
"That just means we’re due as an organization," Freddie Freeman said. "I don’t think any of us are going to be upset with winning 100 games."
The 2026 Dodgers are not just looking to win it all. They are defending their World Series title for the second year in a row, seeking to complete the Majors' first three-peat since the 1998-2000 Yankees.
After the bye week, in which they'll await the outcome of the Wild Card Series between the Braves and Phillies, the Dodgers' title defense begins in earnest in the NL Division Series, starting on Saturday at Dodger Stadium.
The Dodgers may have 100 wins in the books, but everything resets in the postseason. Moving forward, they're focused on getting the 11 wins they need to hoist the Commissioner's Trophy for a third straight year.

- The Dodgers enter October seeking a third straight World Series title, but the club has not settled on a closer despite spending heavily on Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott.
- Andrew Friedman is confident about the Dodgers’ bullpen adapting to late-inning, high-leverage situations in the playoffs no matter who might be called upon.
SAN FRANCISCO — Stop me if you’ve heard this a million times, but the Dodgers are trying to become the first team to win three consecutive World Series championships since the New York Yankees, from 1998 to 2000.
Those Yankees had a Hall of Fame closer. In 1998, Mariano Rivera got the final four outs of the clincher. In 1999, he got the final four outs. In 2000, he got the final three outs.
These Dodgers? Their closer? Your guess is as good as theirs.
“I do not know,” said Andrew Friedman, the Dodgers’ president of baseball operations.
This might be a good time to know, no? The regular season is over. The postseason is upon us.
Alex Call hits a run-scoring double and Andy Pages follows with a three-run home run in the 10th inning of the Dodgers’ 5-1 win over the San Francisco Giants.
“I feel very confident that we’re going to be going into October with arguably the deepest and best pitching staff that we’ve had,” he said. “Exactly what their roles will be and how things will be ordered, I don’t know right now.”
Perhaps the Dodgers are overthinking this. They have done that before.
Tanner Scott converted 25 of 29 save opportunities this season, including saves Friday and Saturday.
But the strongest hitters on the Dodgers’ possible division series opponents are left-handed — Matt Olson, Drake Baldwin and Michael Harris II on the Atlanta Braves; Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber on the Philadelphia Phillies — and the Dodgers may not hesitate to use the left-handed Scott against those guys in the seventh or eighth inning.
In theory, these Dodgers have three candidates as closer: Scott, their marquee closer signing for 2025 and actual closer for most of 2026; Edwin Díaz, their marquee closer signing for 2026; and Roki Sasaki, their accidental closer last October.
Yet Friedman said he could envision scenarios where Evan Phillips could close, or even Brock Stewart, or perhaps Alex Vesia against a run of left-handed hitters. The Dodgers hope to activate Edgardo Henriquez for the playoffs. The starters could close, too, especially a well-rested Tyler Glasnow early in the first round.
Dave Roberts know the Dodgers’ chances of a three-peat rest on a surprise hero giving the team a timely boost. Meet Bill Plaschke’s top candidates for the job.
“We’ve got a number of guys that we really trust,” Friedman said. “Depending on who we’re playing, how deep our starter goes, there are a lot of factors that would go into it. But, more than who will be that pitcher on the mound, is the fact that we have so many candidates we feel really good about.”
That the Dodgers have improvised an October relief corps, transformed a rookie starter into a postseason closer and run bullpen games in elimination games might lead you to conclude Friedman does not really believe in the concept of a designated closer. In a world where “high leverage” is the trendy jargon, maybe a closer is more of an anachronism than a necessity.
That the Dodgers invested $72 million in Scott and $69 million in Díaz in consecutive winters would lead you to conclude Friedman does indeed believe in the concept of a designated closer. In fact, he does.
“I think it’s extremely helpful,” he said.
The Dodgers do not hold splashy news conferences to introduce closer candidates. When the Dodgers introduced Díaz last December, Friedman proudly introduced the three-time All-Star as the closer.
“For us, we have a high bar,” Friedman said then. “To name someone the closer, you have to be one of the best. You have to be elite and dominant at what you do.”
Díaz’s season went awry, limited to 18⅔ innings after elbow surgery and then a neck injury. But in five September appearances since his activation from the injured list, he gave up no runs and one hit in five innings, striking out nine of the 17 batters he faced. (In the same span, Scott has given up no runs and two hits in five innings, striking out nine of the 19 batters he faced.)
“What we’ve seen out of Díaz recently has been really encouraging,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “What that ultimately means, we don’t know yet.
“Of course, if you have a reliever who is really hot in October, that can be extremely valuable. It doesn’t mean you use him exclusively in the ninth. But, by and large, that’s how you would use him.”
Roberts saluted Díaz for working hard to get back to an uncertain assignment.
“I’m really proud of Edwin, given the deal he signed, to work it out, to go to the minors, to come back and pitch in whatever role we ask of him, that shows a lot of character,” Roberts said.
“He could have mailed this year in. That’s something that has not gone unnoticed. And we’ll see how October plays out.”
The Dodgers could be forgiven for believing it will all work out in the end. Their final pitcher in each of the World Series clinchers under Friedman, all starters: Julio Urías in 2020, Walker Buehler in 2024, Yoshinobu Yamamoto in 2025.
The pitchers to record a postseason save in those championship seasons: Kenley Jansen, Joe Kelly, Brusdar Graterol, Blake Treinen and Urias in 2020; Alex Vesia, Treinen and Buehler in 2024; Glasnow, Sasaki and Treinen in 2025.
The organizational flexibility can lead to some uncomfortable discussions within the clubhouse, as Roberts and coaches keep the relievers updated on the latest plan for how they might be used.
“It is tricky,” Roberts said. “These are constant conversations. They are ever-evolving. They are ongoing.”
If all goes right for the Dodgers, those conversations will be ongoing for another month.

SAN FRANCISCO – Well, enough of that – now on to the important stuff.
The Dodgers reached the end of the compulsory phase of their year, finishing the regular season with a 5-1 win in 10 innings against the San Francisco Giants on Sunday afternoon at Oracle Park.
The win was the Dodgers’ 100th of the season. It is the 12th time in franchise history that they have finished a season with 100 wins (including six of the past nine full seasons). None of the previous 100-win regular seasons were followed by a World Series championship.
The Dodgers will now take Monday off before getting together for four days of simulated games, live batting practice and whatever else they deem necessary to get ready for the opening of the postseason that will determine if they can become the first National League franchise to win three consecutive World Series championships.
Game 1 of their NL Division Series will be Saturday at Dodger Stadium against the winner of the Wild Card Series between the Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies. That best-of-three series begins Tuesday in Atlanta – and the Dodgers will be watching.
“There’s going to be some watch parties at the ballpark. I thought that was something that was really good,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said of the bye week itinerary established in 2024. “You’re not playing in the Wild Card Series, but you’re watching it and you kind of get your juices going. There’s also a bonding piece that I think is important.
“I thought we did a good job of having enough live and game situations, simulating them. Our coaches are sort of revisiting what we did a couple years ago. If there’s things we want to improve on or what – it worked out well a couple years ago. A lot of it’s also contingent on how guys are feeling, making sure they get rested and reset.”
MLB’s easiest September schedule allowed the Dodgers to go into their bye week with positive momentum. They went 18-7 in the final month (including 6-0 against the Giants in the final 10 days). Only the San Diego Padres (19-6) had more wins in the month.
Those bye-week sim games essentially started this weekend at Oracle Park.
On Sunday, the Dodgers sent seven pitchers to the mound to get their work. They allowed one run on five hits — and survived giving up the potential game-deciding home run. Giants shortstop Christian Koss took Dodgers reliever Bobby Miller deep leading off the eighth inning — but replay review turned the home run into a foul ball.
Roki Sasaki made his third appearance out of the bullpen since returning from a blister and did nothing to undermine his status as perhaps the most important bullpen weapon the Dodgers will have this postseason. He struck out two of the three batters he faced in a 1-2-3 inning.
Over his three innings in relief, Sasaki has faced 11 batters and struck out six, allowing two hits in his first appearance and none since.
“I think the fastball’s better,” Roberts said, comparing the version of Sasaki the Dodgers got when they moved him to the bullpen last postseason. “I think the split’s better. It’s also nice that he’s already done it. Just in total, he’s just a better pitcher than he was last year and a lot more confident.”
Edwin Diaz continued to affirm his status as a rediscovered bullpen weapon with another 1-2-3 inning. And Roberts reported Edgardo Henriquez has been throwing bullpen sessions this weekend and will participate in the bye week workouts with the expectation that he will be ready to return from his lower back injury and be part of the Dodgers’ NLDS bullpen.
The Dodgers’ offense didn’t spark to life until the 10th inning when Alex Call doubled in the free runner then trotted home on a three-run home run by Andy Pages.

For nine-plus innings, the Dodgers and Giants couldn’t buy a hit with a runner in scoring position, but in the tenth, the Dodgers broke through for a 5-1 win. Alex Call and Andy Pages recorded two-out hits, a double, and a three-run shot to give the Dodgers their first lead in this game and the only one they’d need.
Dodgers find their breakthrough in extras to beat the Giants
Making a habit out of squandering chances through nine innings, the Dodgers scored four in extras to beat the Giants
Before getting to that point of being tied in extras, Jack Dreyer did a reasonable job of keeping the Giants at bay as an opener, but a stolen base allowed the opportunity for just a pair of singles to open the scoring in the second. Shay Whitcomb singled and stole second, later driven in by Scott Bandura—his first RBI of the season, playing in just his 13th big league game. Bandura also tried to steal a base, but this time Dreyer was alert to the danger and picked him off.
Facing a traditional bullpen game with Carson Seymour completing just one inning to open this one, the Dodgers first threatened to score in the third, the inning marked by Tony Vitello’s ejection. With two on and a 2-2 count to Mookie Betts, a check swing in which he probably went around was called a no-swing. Vitello came out to argue what had already been a topic of frustration earlier in the game and was thrown out for the seventh time in his 2026. The Giants, however, got out of the jam, as Betts struck out on the next pitch, and Sam Hentges also punched out Freddie Freeman.
What the Dodgers offense couldn’t do in the third, it did in the following frame. Kyle Tucker got on to leadoff the inning thanks to a defensive error by the second baseman and moved to third on a Max Muncy double—his 27th of the season, setting a new career high in a single season. With two on and one out, Andy Pages evened the score with a sacrifice fly.
Through the following innings, the Dodgers kept threatening but never coming through, first with a Freddie Freeman hit with a man on being taken away by a great defensive play from Jonah Cox—somewhat redeeming himself for the error that contributed to the Dodgers’ first run. That, by the way, would be Freeman’s last action in the game, replaced after five by Kiké Hernández as Dave Roberts rotated key pieces.
In the sixth, Muncy nearly wrote another chapter in his book as a giant killer. But the deepest part of the park was just deep enough to keep him from a solo shot in a ball that would’ve gone out in 23 of 30 stadiums. Perhaps the biggest squandered chance, though, came in the seventh and eighth when the Dodgers first stranded a leadoff double by Tommy Edman with three straight groundouts—an inning later, after Muncy secured his third hit of the day, Andy Pages hit into an inning-ending double play with two on and one out.
The Dodgers’ pitching was the reason the offense kept getting these opportunities to take the lead. Justin Wrobleski was the first pitcher out of the bullpen for the Dodgers, but looking for an even distribution of workload, he only completed two scoreless innings in under 30 pitches. Roki Sasaki and Edwin Díaz combined to strike out three, each with a scoreless frame.
Although Wrobleski had a couple of scares, the Giants truly came back to threaten again in the seventh when Bobby Miller took the mound, but also without actually breaking through. With runners at the corners and no outs, Miller secured a strikeout, then lucked into Marcelo Mayer staying at third on a wild pitch quickly recovered by Hunter Feduccia, recorded another punchout, and finished off the inning with a groundout.
With both teams exhausting new ways of threatening without actually scoring, the Giants looked like they’d take the lead with a leadoff bomb in the eighth by Christian Koss. However, the call on the field of a home run was overturned when replay made it clear it was a foul ball, and the score remained 1-1 through nine innings.
Even in the tenth, it looked like the Dodgers were going to strand the ghost runner after their first two hitters were retired without him advancing to third, but Call came through, and an intentional walk later, Pages had the big hit of the game. With the four RBI he recorded in this game, Pages left Ohtani behind and isolated himself as the Dodgers’ RBI leader this season, with 85.
Sunday particulars
Home run: Andy Pages (23)
WP —Alex Vesia (3-1): 1 IP, 1 hit, 1 strikeout
LP —Duncan Davitt (0-1):1 IP, 2 hits, 4 runs, 3 earned runs, 1 walk
Up next
The Dodgers get a little under a week off before they get back on the field on Saturday at home. They’ll be playing host to the winner of the Wild Card round between the Braves and Phillies in game 1 of the NLDS. No starters have been announced for that series.

The Los Angeles Dodgers have their sights set on winning a third consecutive World Series, which would make them the first team since the New York Yankees, over a quarter century ago, to achieve that feat.
The Dodgers, who are about to open up a series against the rival San Francisco Guardians on the cusp of the MLB postseason, have welcomed back catcher Dalton Rushing off the injured list, but also had to make a corresponding move to open up room on the roster.
The Los Angeles Dodgers Have Optioned Alex Freeland To The Minors
In a corresponding move, the Dodgers have optioned Alex Freeland to the minors, opening up a spot for Rushing.
“The Dodgers have reinstated catcher Dalton Rushing from the injured list and optioned IF Alex Freeland,” the Dodgers reported on X, formerly known as Twitter.
However, the move wasn’t fully well received by fans.
“All Rushing can do is pinch hit. Which means you burn the guy he hits for, Rushing, and a replacement fielder the next inning. Peak Dave Roberts thinking,” one fan noted.
This fan said, “Meaningless series vs. the Giants and could’ve been testing out De Paula in left field this weekend but Alex Call has compromising photos of Friedman apparently.”
This fan said, “Rushing’s elbow is completely fried and this is the second time they’ve recalled him from the IL. I honestly don’t understand it at all.”
Alex Freeland Has Been Optioned To Triple-A By The Dodgers
Freeland was taken by the Dodgers the third round of the 2022 MLB Draft. He began his professional career with Rancho Cucamonga, hitting .313 in eight games, before spending 2023 with Great Lakes, where he batted .240 with nine home runs and 57 RBI.
Freeland climbed through three levels in 2024, finishing the season with Triple-A Oklahoma City. Across 136 games, he hit .260 with 18 homers, 74 RBI and 31 stolen bases.
He started 2025 with Oklahoma City before receiving his first MLB promotion in late July. Freeland debuted for Los Angeles on July 30, collecting his first hit against Cincinnati, and hit his first major-league homer off Yu Darvish on Aug. 22. He hit .190 with two home runs and six RBI in 29 games with the Dodgers, while posting a .263/.384/.451 line with 16 homers and 82 RBI in 106 Triple-A games.
Freeland made the Dodgers’ 2026 Opening Day roster and began the season splitting time at second base with Miguel Rojas.
Freeland has appeared in 89 games so far this season for the Dodgers, and has four home runs with 21 RBI along with a .234 batting average and a .652 OPS.

On Wednesday, the Los Angeles Dodgers reactived Shohei Ohtani from the 15-day IL and optioned Josue De Paula, which was just about the most unpopular decision they could've made.
No one can really complain about having Ohtani back, but De Paula had captured the hearts and attentions of Dodgers fans so quickly that we would've preferred the team make a more drastic measure, like cutting Alex Call, than sending De Paula away for the time being.
There is still a distinct chance that the Dodgers enter a petition with the Commissioner's Office to carry De Paula on their postseason rosters, but fans want every second of the No. 1 prospect they can get.
The Dodgers took the field for the second game of three against the San Diego Padres without their electric rookie, and they certainly played like they'd lost a spark.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto is no stranger to getting little-to-no run support from his team. In the fifth, with the Padres already up 2-0 thanks to a Manny Machado homer, Yamamoto gave up back-to-back singles before a Dustin Harris laid down a bunt. Yamamoto fielded and tried to throw to third to get the lead runner, but it sailed into foul territory, allowing a run to score.
The Dodgers offense, meanwhile, only scored a single run on a Tommy Edman sac fly.
Dodgers clearly already missing their sparkplug after Josue De Paula option, loss to Padres
The Dodgers' loss and an Atlanta Braves win kept LA from clinching the first-round bye that escaped them last year. The Padres' win allowed them to pull away from the rest of the crowded NL Wild Card pack. Going into Wednesday's game, the Padres, Chicago Cubs, and Philadelphia Phillies were all tied with the same 87-70 record. The Phillies also lost, which allowed the Padres to pull away by a game in the standings.
Although the Dodgers clinching is still all but inevitable, fans are getting antsier the further we come down to the wire.
There are still some big questions to be answered when the Dodgers get to October, the De Paula vs. Dalton Rushing debate being one of them. Dave Roberts already admitted that it would be an uphill battle for Rushing, given how well and how immediately De Paula established himself.
The offense's lifeless showing against the Padres on Wednesday might've been an indirect plus in De Paula's column. Look what they turned into without him.

LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers on Tuesday got a few regulars back as reinforcements heading into the final week of the regular season and into October, activating center fielder Andy Pages and pitcher Roki Sasaki off the injured list.
Pages missed 27 games after getting hit by a fastball on his left hand on August 21. Sasaki left his start in Atlanta five days later with a blister on his right middle finger.
Emmet Sheehan and catcher Eliezer Alfonzo were optioned to Triple-A Oklahoma City on Monday.
Pages was an All-Star starter this season, and when he got hurt was tied with Yoshinobu Yamamoto for second-highest FanGraphs WAR (3.9) on the team, behind only Shohei Ohtani. By Baseball Reference WAR, Pages is still third on the team now at 5.4, trailing only Ohtani and Yamamoto. That’ll happen with a .272/.338/.458 batting line with a 118 wRC+ combined with plus-defense in center field.
Before getting hit by an errant fastball on August 21, Pages started 125 of the Dodgers’ 129 games, and led the team in plate appearances (550) at the time. Pages and Ohtani are still tied for the Dodgers’ lead with 80 runs batted in. With Pages out, Alek Thomas was first called up to start six games in center field, followed by Tommy Edman starting 17 games, plus three starts by Alex Call and one by Kiké Hernández.
With Edman moving to the outfield and once Thomas was optioned, Miguel Rojas (10) and Alex Freeland (eight) have covered all but one of the starts at second base in September.
Sasaki struggled earlier in the season, but improved as the season progressed. He has a streak of six straight starts with no more than two runs allowed until his blister start in Atlanta. On the season, Sasaki has a 4.46 ERA and 4.42 xERA, but since July 8 he’s down to a 3.25 ERA and 3.76 xERA in eight starts.
With Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and Tyler Glasnow set for the postseason rotation, the Dodgers will see over the next two weeks if Blake Snell will be hampered by his left groin discomfort, and will have Sheehan at the ready. That allows them to use Sasaki in relief, as they did last postseason out of necessity.
“I could see multiples [innings], but it’s not going to be bulk as in four or five innings,” manager Dave Roberts said on Sunday.
Last season was a different situation for Sasaki, who struggled mightily as a starter and spend four months on the injured list before returning in the final week of the regular season. There was no room in the rotation, so he pitched in relief in the postseason. He wasn’t dominant — only six strikeouts among his 43 batters faced, with five walks — but he was effective, allowing only one run over nine appearances and 10 2/3 innings, the highlight his perfect three innings of relief in the Dodgers’ NLDS Game 4 clincher over the Philadelphia Phillies.
Sasaki saved three games last postseason. Roberts said Sasaki probably wouldn’t get an opportunity in a save situation right away this week, but it could progress to that by the postseason.
“I trust Roki in any situation. I would say probably starting a clean inning,” Roberts said. “He’s done it, he’s really good. He’s a neutral pitcher, high-octane stuff. And you really just need four starters. So we’re in a good spot there, for now.”
Sheehan has been fantastic of late, allowing only one run in three starts for the Dodgers over the previous two weeks, with 24 strikeouts in 17 innings. The plan for Sheehan is to start on Saturday for Oklahoma City should the Comets advance to the Triple-A championship game.
Alfonzo was back with the Dodgers since September 6 when Dalton Rushing was placed on the injured list with elbow soreness. In the 14 games since, Alfonzo played only once, pinch-hitting as the designated hitter at the end of a 14-1 blowout of the Cincinnati Reds. He struck out.
Alfonzo made his major league debut against the Padres on July 5, and started nine games behind the plate. He had five hits in 28 at-bats with three doubles and four runs batted in.

The Los Angeles Dodgers have already clinched their fifth straight National League Division championship and now have their sights set on October, where they hope to become just the third franchise to win three consecutive World Series titles. There’s loads of talent up and down the roster, and there’s also a strong core of believers who are vocal about their faith in God.
Six players — utility man Tommy Edman, star outfielder Mookie Betts, reliever Blake Treinen, starting pitcher Justin Wrobleski, reliever Evan Phillips and outfielder Alex Call — joined team chaplain Brandon Cash for Faith and Family Day on Sunday, where they shared their testimonies and how their faith guides them as professional baseball players. It’s an annual event many teams hold, like the Cleveland Guardians and Pittsburgh Pirates.
All six are regular attendees of team chapels and seen as leaders in the clubhouse as much as they are on the field. Call, for example, was traded from the Washington Nationals to L.A. at the trade deadline last season. Cash said he was excited because he heard Call was the spiritual leader in the Washington clubhouse, and he’s since carried that over to the Dodgers.
His testimony mirrored many of his teammates’ in a lot of ways in that he grew up in church with parents who modeled what it looked like to have a strong faith. Like a lot of believers, once he was on his own in college and then as a professional player, he had to decide if his faith was his own or just something he believed because his parents did.
“That’s where it kind of became real for me,” Call said. “I went from, ‘Yeah, I don’t do this or this because I’m a Christian’ to ‘God calls us all to be disciple makers. He calls us all to love and to be a blessing.’ That’s where I turned it up a notch and try not to be ashamed of the Gospel or anything else — just glorify Jesus in my daily life and on the field.”
Wrobleski had a similar upbringing thanks to a mother who set an example and raised him in the faith.
“It’s been a journey for me,” he said. “I’d be lying if I didn’t say there were ups and downs with my faith and God trying to show me things and get me back to where I need to be. Every time I feel like I’ve been down in my life or I feel like things aren’t going the way that I want, it’s just God showing me I need to get back to the Word and pray.”
A first-time All-Star this year, Wrobleski has been a pleasant surprise for the Dodgers and a mainstay in the rotation, making 22 starts with a 3.70 ERA. The Dodgers could use him either in the rotation or as a long reliever in the postseason like last year.
He shared that a verse that’s stuck with him lately is Romans 12:12, which says, “Be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, faithful in prayer.”
“That’s something I’m trying to live out right now,” he said. “It’s a journey. Knowing Jesus obviously gives you that peace when you’re out there. For me, it’s big before the game. It’s a super big blessing to pitch for the Dodgers, but there’s a lot of pressure that comes with it. Just knowing that the results aren’t always what matters; it’s just giving your performance to the Lord, good or bad, and that’s kind of been something I’m trying to do this year.”
That pressure is felt by all the players. They know the expectations that come with playing in L.A. They know their team is loaded with talent and high-priced players.
Edman — who shared that his faith grew substantially when he was in college at Stanford thanks to faith mentors and involvement in the Fellowship of Christian Athletes — said he handles the scrutiny of playing pro baseball by remembering that his identity is in Christ.
“As a baseball player, one of the big struggles that we have is our identity being tied up in our performance on the field or being just a baseball player,” Edman said. “Baseball is such a crazy long season and a rollercoaster of emotions that you can go up and down like crazy.
“I have my identity rooted in my role as a son of God and a follower of Jesus Christ. I always have that in my foundation. Not to say that helps me perform on the field, but it definitely allows me to have that inner peace regardless of how I’ve done on the baseball field.”

Each player has a different background that led them to where they are personally and professionally, and that’s something that makes the chapel dynamic unique, Cash said. For example, Betts didn’t really grow up in the church like some of his teammates did. He spent most of his weekends playing baseball, and going to church just wasn’t much of a priority.
“As I got a little older playing ball, I kind of wanted the sense of purpose, because ball is just an avenue to show what God has given me and given all of us,” said Betts, an eight-time All-Star. “Once I wanted to learn my purpose, I think going to chapel, getting to know Cash, getting to know these guys has really changed my life completely. These are literally like my brothers. Obviously we’ve grown playing baseball and winning together, but I think we’ve grown the most in our Bible studies and our chapels on Sundays.”
He said he just read through 1 and 2 Kings, where he read about King Soloman and how he was wise and felt on top of the world. Betts saw some similarities to pro baseball.
“When you’re on top of the world and everything’s going great, but you lose what’s important, which is God, you kind of lose everything,” he said. “No matter how good or bad I do, I make sure to give glory to God and I make sure that every day I pray and give glory to Him because everything we have here is for Him.”

Treinen, who’s now in his seventh season with the Dodgers, shared that he sort of begrudgingly attended church growing up. His mother was a member of the worship team, which meant he often spent all morning and part of the afternoon at church when he would’ve rather been home watching football.
“As I’ve gotten older, I’ve greatly appreciated the stubbornness and consistency that my mom put in my life for me and my brother to take us to church on Sunday,” he said. “It was a lot as a kid, but it built a structure of faith and a standard of worship in life.”
He recalled a moment at a youth conference at the University of Tennessee where he said he “felt the tangible presence of the Holy Spirit just rock me and put me in my seat.” He recounted how Christians should always be able to give an answer for the hope they have in Jesus, and that experience is what he goes back to when explaining where he first believed.
“We all have the right to believe what we want,” he said. “But when you see the truth and the facts and the tangible hand of God in your life, it separates just wanting to be a good person and knowing Jesus is real, to ‘this is absolute.’ I’ve experienced the presence of the Father and I will forever with my life.”
